sections.heading: How it works
sections.order_note: Teaching order follows one request and then one packet: the request reaches an edge location and a miss climbs to the origin (1); the path picks a behavior and its origin (2); the cache key decides sharing (3); headers decide how long a copy lives (4); the origin is locked: S3 (5), load balancers and other origins (6); both legs are encrypted (7); signed access decides which users get private files (8); code can run at the edge (9); a second origin takes over (10). sections.heading: Requests reach the nearest edge location and cache misses travel on to the origin

plan.problem: Users far from your Region wait for every byte to cross the internet, and every request loads the origin. A copy of the content must sit close to the users.
trace: **Send the configuration.** After you create a distribution, CloudFront sends the [distribution's configuration (but not your content)] to its edge locations (cloudfront-config-sent-to-edge-not-content). Content arrives only when someone asks for it.
**Pick an edge location.** [DNS routes the request to the CloudFront POP] that can best serve it, typically the [nearest CloudFront POP in terms of latency] (cloudfront-dns-routes-to-pop).
**Check the cache.** If the object is in the cache, [CloudFront returns it to the user] (cloudfront-cache-hit-returns-from-edge).

**Climb on a miss.** The request goes on to a regional edge cache, [located between your origin server and the POPs], with a [larger cache than an individual POP] (cloudfront-rec-between-pop-and-origin, cloudfront-rec-larger-cache-than-pop); on a second miss CloudFront [forwards the request to your origin server] (cloudfront-cache-miss-forwards-to-origin).
**Stream and keep.** [As soon as the first byte arrives], CloudFront forwards it to the user and [adds the object to the cache] (cloudfront-first-byte-forwarded-and-cached).
plan.table: Truth table, columns Case | Answered by | Requests to the origin: hit at the edge location | the edge location | none; miss at the edge location, hit in the regional edge cache | the regional edge cache | none; miss in both | the origin, then both caches keep a copy | one, even when many viewers ask for the same object at the same moment ([This brief pause helps to reduce the load], cloudfront-request-collapsing). Keep cells at or under 15 words.
plan.why: Why build layers? An edge location is small; [POPs in a region share a local cache] (cloudfront-rec-shared-cache-persistent-connections), so a miss in one city can still be a hit in the shared layer before your servers see it.
plan.exam_signal: 'users around the world see slow page loads' points to CloudFront, which AWS suggests for [any publicly accessible web application] (cloudfront-dec-consider-for-any-public-web-application); it also speeds up [dynamic, uncacheable workloads like APIs] (cloudfront-dec-dynamic-uncacheable-still-faster). Strict after the quoted phrase.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: requests that skip the regional edge cache. At most 75 words. Proxy methods such as PUT and POST [go directly to the origin from the POPs] (cloudfront-rec-proxy-methods-skip); dynamic requests [do not flow through regional edge caches] (cloudfront-rec-dynamic-requests-skip); and for an S3 origin in the same Region as the best regional edge cache, [the POP skips the regional edge cache] (cloudfront-rec-skipped-same-region-s3). The regional edge cache is [enabled by default] at [no additional charges] (cloudfront-faq-regional-edge-cache-default-on-no-charge).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the nearest edge location answers from its cache. The thing to watch is that a miss still reaches your origin. (at most 25 words, no absolute word)
plan.stop_and_answer: 'Two users near the same edge location ask for the same new file at the same moment, before CloudFront has a copy. How many requests reach the origin?' Answer: 'One. CloudFront holds the second request and [sends the response from the original request] to both (cloudfront-request-collapsing).' The table mentions the pause; the prompt applies it to a concrete case.

sections.heading: Cache behaviors send each URL path to one origin and the first match wins

plan.problem: One website keeps its static files in a bucket and its API behind a load balancer. One domain name must reach both, and only the files should be cached.
trace: **List the origins.** A distribution can use an S3 bucket, an Application Load Balancer or [an AWS Lambda function URL] (cloudfront-origin-kinds), and [any origin server] outside AWS (cloudfront-faq-custom-origin-any-server-no-charge).

**Match the path.** CloudFront compares the request path [compared with path patterns in the order] of the behaviors; [The first match determines which cache behavior] applies (cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins). It [does not consider query strings or cookies] for this (cloudfront-behavior-path-pattern-ignores-query-cookies).

**Fall back to the default.** The default behavior is [always the last to be processed] (cloudfront-behavior-default-last); its pattern * [cannot be changed] (cloudfront-behavior-default-path-pattern-fixed).
**Use one origin.** In each behavior [you specify the one origin] (cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each).

**Cache or pass through.** CloudFront [caches responses to GET and HEAD requests], not [requests that use other methods] (cloudfront-methods-cached); [POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH requests] go on to the origin (cloudfront-faq-post-put-delete-patch-not-cached).
plan.table: Example distribution, columns Order | Path pattern | Origin | Caching: 1 | /static/* | S3 bucket | CachingOptimized; 2 | /api/* | Application Load Balancer | CachingDisabled ([This policy disables caching], cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled); last | * (default) | Application Load Balancer | per page. A design example; no AWS number in cells.
plan.why: Why one origin per behavior? Each path then has one place to fetch from and one caching rule, so one distribution can cache images and pass API calls through.
plan.exam_signal: 'one domain name for static files in Amazon S3 and dynamic content on EC2' points to one distribution with a cache behavior for each path pattern, where [you specify the one origin] (cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each).
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A distribution lists two behaviors in this order: 1 '*.jpg' to the photo bucket, with no signer; 2 '/premium/*' to the same bucket, with a trusted key group for signed URLs. What is wrong? Reveal (about 60 words with the prompt): a request for /premium/photo.jpg matches '*.jpg' first, because [The first match determines which cache behavior] applies (cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins), and signed URLs are needed only for the files of a behavior that has a signer ([As soon as you add the signer], cloudfront-signer-added-requires-signed-access). Premium photos are free. Fix: list '/premium/*' first.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: each path pattern picks one origin and one caching rule. The thing to watch is the order, because the first match wins.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A distribution lists /api/* first and /api/v2/* second, with different origins. Which origin answers /api/v2/users?' Answer: 'The origin of /api/*: [The first match determines which cache behavior] applies (cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins). List the longer pattern first.'

sections.heading: The cache key decides which requests share one cached copy

plan.problem: Two users ask for the same page. If CloudFront sees two different requests, both go to the origin, and the cache helps nobody.
trace: **Build the key.** A cache policy sets the values [included in the cache key]: query strings, headers and cookies (cloudfront-cache-policy-controls-cache-key).
**Look up the key.** Requests with the same key share one copy; the share answered from the cache is [the cache hit ratio] (cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-definition).

**Forward what the origin needs.** Values in the key [are automatically included in origin requests] (cloudfront-cache-key-values-forwarded-to-origin); other viewer values [is not included in the origin request] by default (cloudfront-origin-request-default-not-forwarded). Note to writer: this display needs a sentence around it that reads well, for example 'by default, a viewer value that is not in the key [is not included in the origin request]'.

**Add values without splitting.** An origin request policy sends extra values to the origin [but *not* include in the cache key] (cloudfront-cache-key-values-forwarded-to-origin); it needs a cache policy in the same behavior ([You cannot use an origin request policy], cloudfront-origin-request-policy-needs-cache-policy). If no display reads well, request one (needs-display).
plan.table: Managed policies, columns Policy | Cache key | Use it for: CachingOptimized | [only includes the normalized Accept-Encoding header], no query strings or cookies (cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-optimized) | static files; CachingDisabled | nothing is cached ([This policy disables caching]) | dynamic content ([useful for dynamic content], cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled).
plan.why: Why keep the key small? Each value in the key can make another copy of the same object, so fewer requests find a match. AWS says to [forward only the query string parameters] that change the response (cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values).
plan.exam_signal: 'the cache hit ratio is low and the origin is overloaded' points to a smaller cache key, [forward only specified cookies instead of forwarding all] (cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values), and to Origin Shield, [an additional layer of caching in front] of the origin that can [improve the cache hit ratio] (cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-origin-shield-layer).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: put in the cache key only what changes the response. The thing to watch is cookies and headers that differ for each user.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'An S3 origin serves product images. The cache policy puts the session cookie in the cache key. What happens to the cache hit ratio, and does S3 use the cookie?' Answer: 'The hit ratio falls, because CloudFront [considers the forwarded cookie values] (cloudfront-faq-forwarded-cookies-part-of-cache-key) and every user has a different session cookie; and [Amazon S3 doesn't process cookies] (cloudfront-s3-origin-ignores-cookies). Remove the cookie from the key.'

sections.heading: Cache headers decide how long a copy lives and versioned names replace it sooner

plan.problem: A release changes app.js at the origin, but users keep getting the old copy from the edge. The copy lives on until something ends it.
trace: **Read the origin's headers.** If the origin sends both, CloudFront [uses only the value of Cache-Control max-age] (cloudfront-expiration-cache-control-over-expires); the Maximum TTL applies when the origin sends [Cache-Control or Expires headers] (cloudfront-ttl-max-ttl-only-with-headers).

**Fall back to Default TTL.** Without those headers the copy lives the Default TTL, [86400 seconds] unless you change it (cloudfront-default-ttl-default-value, cloudfront-ttl-default-ttl-only-without-headers).
**Respect the floor.** If the [minimum TTL is greater than 0], CloudFront caches for at least that time, even with no-cache, [no-store, or private] (cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache).
**Check again after expiry.** The next request asks the origin, which answers [304 Not Modified] or [200 OK] with the new file (cloudfront-expiration-304-not-modified-revalidation).

**Replace it early.** A new file name needs no waiting, and [you don't have to pay for object invalidation] (cloudfront-versioned-file-names-recommended); an invalidation removes the old name: [Invalidate the file from edge caches] (cloudfront-invalidate-removes-from-edge-caches).
plan.table: Ways to update, columns Way | What it costs | Also fixes browser caches: wait for the TTL | nothing | yes, after expiry; invalidate the path | [first 1,000 invalidation paths] each month free (cloudfront-invalidation-first-1000-paths-free), a wildcard [counts as one path] (cloudfront-invalidation-wildcard-counts-one-path) | edge caches only; versioned file name | nothing extra | yes: versioning controls copies [cached locally or behind a corporate proxy] is the idea; link [Versioning is less expensive] (cloudfront-invalidation-prefer-versioning-for-frequent-updates) and keep the browser claim inside that fact's scope.
plan.why: Why prefer new names? A new name is a new object for every cache at once, edge, browser and proxy, so no old copy can answer for it. AWS says [we recommend that you primarily use file versioning] for frequent updates (cloudfront-invalidation-prefer-versioning-for-frequent-updates).
plan.exam_signal: 'files are updated frequently and users must see the new version' points to versioned file names ([we recommend that you primarily use file versioning]); 'remove harmful content now' points to the [Invalidation API] (cloudfront-faq-remove-item-delete-origin-or-invalidate).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: invalidation details and stale copies. At most 75 words. [Invalidation paths are case sensitive] (cloudfront-invalidation-paths-case-sensitive); if CloudFront forwards query strings, [you must include the query strings when invalidating] (cloudfront-invalidation-include-query-strings); an invalidation [invalidates every cached version of the file regardless] of cookies (cloudfront-invalidation-all-cached-versions-cookies). CloudFront also [supports tag invalidations] (cloudfront-invalidation-by-cache-tags). With Stale-If-Error, CloudFront can serve an expired copy [if the origin is unreachable or returns] an error (cloudfront-stale-if-error-behavior).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: give each release new file names. The thing to watch is the Default TTL when the origin sends no cache headers.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'The origin sends no Cache-Control or Expires header, and the cache behavior keeps its default TTL settings. A file changes at 09:00. For how long can a user still get the old copy?' Answer: 'Until the cached copy is a day old: CloudFront uses the Default TTL, [86400 seconds] (cloudfront-default-ttl-default-value), [only when the origin does *not* send] those headers (cloudfront-ttl-default-ttl-only-without-headers).'

sections.heading: Origin access control keeps the bucket private and lets your distribution read it

plan.problem: The recordings must stay in a private bucket, but CloudFront has to read them. Users must not skip CloudFront by opening an S3 URL.
trace: **Create an origin access control** and attach it to the S3 origin. AWS offers OAC and the older origin access identity (OAI): [We recommend that you use OAC instead] (cloudfront-oac-oai-two-ways-oac-recommended).

**Sign every request.** With the recommended setting, [CloudFront always signs all requests] that it sends to the bucket (cloudfront-oac-signing-always-recommended), and they travel [always through HTTPS] (cloudfront-oac-always-https-when-signing).

**Allow the service, for one distribution.** The bucket policy allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)], and a Condition allows it [only when the request is on behalf] of your distribution (cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).
**Keep the bucket private.** Viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs] (cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
plan.table: Signing setting, columns Setting | The bucket must be | Result: Sign requests (recommended) | private, with a policy for the distribution | CloudFront reads; S3 URLs fail ([This prevents someone from bypassing CloudFront], cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls); Do not sign requests | public: [the S3 bucket origin must be publicly accessible] (cloudfront-oac-never-sign-needs-public-bucket) | anyone can open S3 URLs.
plan.why: Why name the distribution in the Condition? Without it, the policy would trust the CloudFront service as a whole, not your distribution. Do not say that other customers could read the bucket: no fact says it.
plan.exam_signal: 'users must reach the files only through CloudFront' points to origin access control on the S3 origin; AWS still documents OAI, but [We recommend that you use OAC instead] (cloudfront-oac-oai-two-ways-oac-recommended).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: OAI, website endpoints and other origins. At most 75 words. OAI [it doesn't work for all scenarios], for example [Dynamic requests (PUT, POST, or DELETE) to Amazon S3] (cloudfront-oai-legacy-not-for-all-scenarios), and for SSE-KMS website buckets [you must use OAC instead] (s3-website-sse-kms-needs-cloudfront-oac). To move, first [allow both the OAI and the distribution] (cloudfront-oai-migrate-allow-both-in-bucket-policy). An S3 website endpoint is [also considered a custom origin], so [you can't use OAC (or OAI)] (cloudfront-oac-s3-website-endpoint-not-supported). OAC also covers [restricting access to a Lambda function URL origin] (cloudfront-oac-lambda-function-url).
plan.try_it: > **Try it:** one sentence: build a private bucket behind a distribution and watch the bucket policy decide. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: cloudfront-t04 -->
plan.say_it: The short answer is: no, the bucket stays private and trusts your distribution. The thing to watch is the Condition that names your distribution.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team sets its origin access control to Do not sign requests and keeps the bucket private. What do viewers get?' Answer: 'Errors. With that setting [the S3 bucket origin must be publicly accessible]; with a private bucket [CloudFront cannot access the origin] and passes the S3 errors on to viewers (cloudfront-oac-never-sign-needs-public-bucket).'

sections.heading: VPC origins let CloudFront reach load balancers and instances in private subnets

plan.problem: An internet-facing load balancer behind CloudFront can still be called directly. Direct calls skip the cache and every protection at the edge.
trace: **Create a VPC origin** for an [Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet] (cloudfront-origin-private-subnet-vpc-origin).
**CloudFront joins the subnet** with a [service-managed elastic network interface (ENI)], which needs [at least one available IPv4 address] there (cloudfront-vpc-origin-private-subnet-ipv4-eni).

**Keep an internet gateway on the VPC.** [You need to add an internet gateway], although it is [not used for routing traffic to origins inside] the subnet (cloudfront-vpc-origin-needs-internet-gateway).
**Serve through one door.** CloudFront is now the way in, [making CloudFront the single point of entry] (cloudfront-vpc-origin-cloudfront-single-entry-point).
plan.table: Truth table, columns Origin | How it accepts only CloudFront: S3 bucket | origin access control (previous subsection); ALB, NLB or EC2 instance that can be private | VPC origin; internet-facing ALB | security group with the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront] (elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), plus a header that CloudFront adds ([add a custom HTTP header to requests], cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https); server outside AWS | custom headers or origin mutual TLS ([origins hosted outside AWS or public origins], cloudfront-faq-origin-mtls-replaces-allowlists-headers). Then embed the ladder cloudfront-origin-lock-ladder after the table (alt, caption = claim).
plan.why: Why a private subnet? A load balancer with no public address gives a direct caller nothing to reach.
plan.exam_signal: 'the load balancer must not be reachable from the internet' points to an internal load balancer as a VPC origin: CloudFront works with [internal Application Load Balancers inside private subnets] (cloudfront-alb-internal-needs-vpc-origins).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: keep the load balancer in private subnets and add it as a VPC origin. The thing to watch is the internet gateway that the VPC still needs.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team wants to add a Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener as a VPC origin. Will that work?' Answer: 'No. [Network Load Balancers with TLS listeners cannot be] VPC origins (cloudfront-vpc-origin-gwlb-and-nlb-tls-not-allowed).' Do not add a fix that no fact gives.

sections.heading: CloudFront encrypts two separate connections and each one has its own setting

plan.problem: A request crosses two networks: the internet to the edge location, then the path from the edge to your origin. Each crossing needs its own encryption.
trace: **Viewer leg.** The viewer protocol policy can redirect, so that [HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS requests] (cloudfront-vpp-redirect-http-to-https), or be [HTTPS Only] (cloudfront-vpp-https-only), which answers an HTTP request with [403 (Forbidden)] (cloudfront-https-only-returns-403).

**Show a certificate for your name.** [The certificate must cover the alternate domain name] (cloudfront-cert-alternate-domain-covered-by-san). An ACM certificate for CloudFront lives in [US East (N. Virginia)] (acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), and [ACM manages certificate renewals for you] (cloudfront-cert-acm-managed-renewal).
**Origin leg.** For a custom origin, the origin protocol policy [HTTPS only] means [CloudFront uses only HTTPS to access the origin] (cloudfront-origin-protocol-https-only).

**Check the origin certificate.** It comes from a trusted authority: [You can’t use a self-signed certificate] (cloudfront-https-origin-trusted-ca-no-self-signed); if no name in it matches the origin domain, the viewer gets [`502 (Bad Gateway)` to the viewer] (cloudfront-https-origin-domain-must-match).
plan.table: Truth table, columns Viewer policy | Origin policy | Encrypted all the way: HTTPS Only | HTTP only | no, the origin leg is plain HTTP; Redirect HTTP to HTTPS | HTTPS only | yes; HTTPS Only | Match viewer | yes, [depending on the protocol of the viewer request] (cloudfront-origin-protocol-match-viewer); any | S3 website endpoint origin | no: [you can't configure CloudFront to use HTTPS] (cloudfront-https-s3-website-no-https-to-origin).
plan.why: Why two settings? CloudFront [terminates TLS close to viewers] (cloudfront-pricing-page-dynamic-acceleration-mechanisms) and opens its own connection to the origin, so each leg is a separate choice.
plan.exam_signal: 'encrypt all data in transit between users and the origin' points to both settings: [require that viewers use HTTPS] and [use HTTPS to get files from your origin] (cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: SNI, dedicated IP addresses and field-level encryption. At most 75 words. With SNI, [virtually all modern web browsers and clients can] connect (cloudfront-sni-recommended-modern-clients), [available at no additional cost] (cloudfront-faq-sni-custom-ssl-modern-browsers-no-extra-cost); for old clients without SNI, dedicated IP addresses cost extra: [you incur an additional monthly charge] (cloudfront-dedicated-ip-legacy-clients-extra-charge). Field-level encryption [adds an additional layer of security] (cloudfront-fle-layer-on-https-selected-fields): the edge encrypts chosen form fields with your public key, and [only your private key can do that] decryption (cloudfront-fle-asymmetric-public-key).
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** The application runs in eu-west-1. A team requests an ACM certificate for www.example.com in eu-west-1, attaches it to the Application Load Balancer, and then tries to choose the same certificate for the CloudFront distribution. What is wrong? Reveal (about 60 words with the prompt): CloudFront needs an ACM certificate in [US East (N. Virginia)] (acm-cloudfront-us-east-1); the load balancer can keep its own, because for the origin you can [import the certificate in any AWS Region] (acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region). Request a second certificate in us-east-1. Trap reused: secrets-certificates-trap-cloudfront-certificate-any-region (no trap comment needed here; it is chapter 07's id).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: set HTTPS for viewers and for the origin, one by one. The thing to watch is the certificate Region for CloudFront.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team switches the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only, but the origin shows a self-signed certificate. What does the viewer get?' Answer: 'An error page: CloudFront [drops the TCP connection] and returns [HTTP status code 502 (Bad Gateway)] (cloudfront-https-origin-bad-certificate-502).'

sections.heading: Signed URLs and signed cookies decide which users can fetch private files

plan.problem: Origin access control stops direct S3 access, but every visitor of the site can still fetch every file through CloudFront. Paid recordings need a check for each user.
trace: **Create a signer.** Use [a trusted key group that you create] in CloudFront; [We recommend that you use trusted key groups] (cloudfront-signer-key-group-recommended), because a root user key pair means [you have to use the AWS Management Console] (cloudfront-signer-root-key-pair-console-only).
**Protect a behavior.** [As soon as you add the signer] to a cache behavior, its files need a signed URL or signed cookie (cloudfront-signer-added-requires-signed-access).

**Sign after sign-in.** Your application signs a URL or sets cookies with [An ending date and time] and, if you want, [The IP address or range of addresses] (cloudfront-dec-signed-url-expiry-restrictions).

**Check at the edge.** CloudFront delivers the file only after [securely signing your requests] checks out (cloudfront-faq-private-content-signed-requests); write the sentence so that the display reads naturally.
plan.table: Truth table, columns Need | Use: one file, or a client without cookies | signed URL ([restrict access to individual files], cloudfront-signed-url-when-individual-files-or-no-cookies); many files such as one HLS video, or URLs that must not change | signed cookies ([access to multiple restricted files], cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls); a start time or an IP range | custom policy ([You can specify the IP address or range], cloudfront-signed-policy-canned-only-expiry); a whole country | geographic restriction: [Geographic restrictions apply to an entire distribution] (cloudfront-geo-restriction-country-level-whole-distribution).
plan.why: Why sign in your application? Only your application knows who paid. It signs with a private key, and CloudFront checks the signature with the public keys of your key group.
plan.exam_signal: 'only paying subscribers can download the files, for a limited time' points to signed URLs or signed cookies, for example for [users who have paid a fee] (cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users); an S3 presigned URL instead sends the user to S3 with the credentials of the [principal who generated the URL] (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: your application signs a link after sign-in, and CloudFront checks it. The thing to watch is the expiry time.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A viewer sends a request with a valid signed cookie and an expired signed URL for the same file. Does CloudFront serve the file?' Answer: 'No. [Signed URLs take precedence over signed cookies], so CloudFront decides [based only on the signed URL] (cloudfront-signed-url-takes-precedence-over-cookies).'

sections.heading: CloudFront Functions do light rewrites and edge Lambda functions can call other services

plan.problem: Each request needs a small decision at the edge: add a header, rewrite a URL or check a token. The code must not slow down every request.
trace: **Pick the event.** Lambda@Edge runs on four events, from [Viewer Request] to [Origin Response] (cloudfront-faq-lambda-edge-four-trigger-events); CloudFront Functions run on the viewer events only, not on [Origin request] (lambda-edge-event-sources-row).

**Know when each event runs.** A viewer request runs [before it checks to see whether the requested] object is cached (cloudfront-lambda-edge-viewer-request-before-cache); an origin request runs [executes *only* when CloudFront forwards a request] to the origin (cloudfront-lambda-edge-origin-request-only-on-miss). Rephrase around the displays so that the sentence reads well.

**Light work: CloudFront Functions.** [Header manipulation], [URL redirects or rewrites] and [Request authorization] (cloudfront-functions-use-cases), in [Submillisecond] time (cloudfront-edge-compare-duration), at [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge] (cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).

**Heavy work: Lambda@Edge.** It can [make network calls to external resources] (cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed) and run [Up to 30 seconds] (cloudfront-edge-compare-duration); the function [must be in the US East (N. Virginia)] Region (cloudfront-lambda-edge-region-must-be-us-east-1).
plan.table: Truth table by task, columns Task | Runs in | Because: add security headers | CloudFront Functions | [Header manipulation] (cloudfront-dec-functions-use-header-manipulation); check a JSON web token | CloudFront Functions | [validate authorization tokens] (cloudfront-dec-functions-use-token-validation); look up the user in a database | Lambda@Edge | [make network calls to external resources]; read the request body | Lambda@Edge | CloudFront Functions have no [Access to the request body] (cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access). Do not repeat the fast file's comparison table.
plan.why: Why two products? A [Submillisecond] function can run on every request and scale to [millions of requests per second] (cloudfront-edge-compare-scale); code that waits on the network needs a runtime that can run longer.
plan.exam_signal: 'lightweight header or URL changes at high scale, MOST cost-effectively' points to CloudFront Functions ([Header manipulation]); 'call an external service before forwarding' points to Lambda@Edge, which can [make network calls to external resources] (cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed).
plan.try_it: > **Try it:** one sentence: test a CloudFront function without a distribution, then try to make it call the network. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: cloudfront-t02 -->
plan.say_it: The short answer is: CloudFront Functions for small rewrites, Lambda@Edge when the code calls other services. The thing to watch is the extra latency of Lambda@Edge.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A function must add a header to the origin's response and must call a pricing API to choose its value. Which product fits?' Answer: 'Lambda@Edge. CloudFront Functions do not run on the [Origin request] or origin response events (lambda-edge-event-sources-row), and they have no [Network access] (cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access).'

sections.heading: An origin group fails over to a second origin when the first one fails

plan.problem: A static site lives in one bucket in one Region. If that Region has a problem, viewers get errors even though CloudFront itself is healthy.
trace: **Create an origin group.** Start with [a distribution with at least two origins], then group them with one as the primary (cloudfront-failover-needs-two-origins).
**Try the primary every time.** CloudFront [routes all incoming requests to the primary origin] (cloudfront-failover-primary-first-every-request).

**Fail over on your codes.** If the primary is unavailable or returns a code that you chose from [400, 403, 404, 416, 429, 500, 502, 503, or 504] (cloudfront-failover-status-codes-you-choose), [CloudFront automatically switches to the secondary origin] (cloudfront-failover-switches-to-secondary).
**Reads only.** This happens [only when the HTTP method of the viewer] request is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS (cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options).
**Mind the wait.** By default CloudFront waits [30 seconds] before it tries the secondary (cloudfront-default-connect-wait-before-failover); fewer attempts or a shorter timeout make it faster.
plan.table: Truth table, columns Request | Primary answers | Viewer gets: GET | 503, a failover code | the secondary origin's answer; GET | 200 | the primary origin's answer; POST | 503 | the 503, because CloudFront [does not fail over when the viewer sends] other methods (cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options).
plan.why: Why automatic failover? During a control plane problem, [origin failovers] keep working (cloudfront-control-plane-impairment-failover-continues), while editing the distribution by hand would [depend on the CloudFront control plane] (cloudfront-static-stability-use-origin-failover-not-manual).
plan.exam_signal: 'serve the static website from a second Region if the first one fails' points to an origin group: for each origin you can [assign a backup origin] (cloudfront-faq-origin-failover-backup-origin).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: an origin group retries a second origin on the error codes that you choose. The thing to watch is that writes do not fail over.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'During an outage of the primary origin, one user opens three pages in a row. Does CloudFront remember the failure and go straight to the secondary for the third page?' Answer: 'No. CloudFront [routes all incoming requests to the primary origin] first, every time (cloudfront-failover-primary-first-every-request), so each page waits for the primary to fail.'

sections.heading: Global Accelerator carries TCP and UDP from two static addresses over the AWS network

plan.problem: Players around the world send UDP game traffic to servers in two Regions. The public internet adds delay and jitter, and partners' firewalls need fixed addresses.
trace: **Get two addresses.** A new accelerator gets [two IPv4 static IP addresses] from [independent network zones] (global-accelerator-faq-two-static-ipv4-independent-network-zones), [anycast from the AWS edge network] (global-accelerator-static-ips-anycast-from-edge).

**Enter at the nearest edge.** Anycast [routes traffic to the closest edge location] (global-accelerator-anycast-nearest-edge-then-closest-endpoint), where Global Accelerator [terminates TCP connections from clients at AWS edge] locations (global-accelerator-terminates-tcp-at-edge).
**Match a listener.** [A listener can be configured for TCP, UDP,] or both, on the ports you choose (global-accelerator-listener-tcp-udp-ports).

**Choose a Region.** A listener has endpoint groups, [each endpoint group with one AWS Region] (global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region); endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers], EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses (global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types).
**Stay on the AWS network** to the endpoint: the [well-monitored, congestion-free, redundant AWS global network] (global-accelerator-traffic-on-aws-network-congestion-free).
plan.table: Truth table, columns Fixed address | Works with | Announced from: Elastic IP address | [tied to a single AWS resource] in one Region | [advertised from a single AWS Region]; Global Accelerator static IP address | endpoints [in any number of AWS Regions] | AWS edge locations (all three displays: global-accelerator-faq-vs-elastic-ip-scope-and-advertisement). Then embed the compare diagram cloudfront-ga-compare (alt, caption = claim).
plan.why: Why anycast? The same two addresses are announced from many edge locations, so each user enters the AWS network close to home, and you can [move endpoints between Availability Zones or AWS Regions] without new addresses (global-accelerator-faq-move-endpoints-without-dns-change).
plan.exam_signal: 'UDP', 'gaming', 'VoIP' or 'fixed IP addresses that partners allow-list' points to Global Accelerator, a good fit for [gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP] (global-accelerator-faq-good-fit-non-http-static-ip-fast-failover).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: client IP preservation and custom routing. At most 75 words. Global Accelerator can keep the client's source address for [Application Load Balancers, Amazon EC2 instances, and Network Load Balancers with security groups] (global-accelerator-client-ip-preservation-three-endpoint-types). A custom routing accelerator [maps listener port ranges to EC2 instance destinations] (global-accelerator-custom-routing-maps-ports-deterministically), for example to [assign multiple players to a single session] (global-accelerator-custom-routing-use-cases-gaming-voip); [Health checks aren't used with custom routing accelerators] (global-accelerator-custom-routing-no-health-checks-no-failover).
plan.try_it: > **Try it:** one sentence: create an accelerator in CloudShell, read its two addresses, then disable it and read them again. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: cloudfront-t03 -->
plan.say_it: The short answer is: two fixed addresses bring TCP or UDP onto the AWS network near users. The thing to watch is that each endpoint group serves one Region.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team disables its accelerator for a week of tests. Must its partners update their allow-lists when the team enables it again?' Answer: 'No. The addresses [remain assigned to your accelerator for as long] as it exists, even when it is disabled; only deleting it loses them (global-accelerator-static-ips-kept-until-delete).'

sections.heading: Health checks and traffic dials move new connections from one Region to another

plan.problem: The application runs in two Regions. When one Region fails, users must move to the other within seconds, not after their DNS caches expire.
trace: **Watch the endpoints.** Global Accelerator [continuously monitors the health of all endpoints] (global-accelerator-health-checks-standard-failover-new-connections); its own health check options are [used for Amazon EC2 and Elastic IP address health checks], [but not for health checks on load balancer] endpoints, which come from Elastic Load Balancing (global-accelerator-elb-health-checks-configured-in-elb).

**Take a failed endpoint out** in [less than one minute] (global-accelerator-faq-failover-detect-under-one-minute), and [instantly begins directing traffic for all new connections] to another endpoint (global-accelerator-health-checks-standard-failover-new-connections).

**Move between Regions.** When a Region fails, it [redirects traffic to the next optimal AWS Region] (global-accelerator-faq-multi-region-failover-redirects-traffic); the addresses do not change, so [Change propagation takes a matter of seconds] (global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds).

**Steer on purpose.** Each endpoint group has a traffic dial, by default [100%]; [set the traffic dial to 0] to cut a Region off for maintenance (global-accelerator-faq-traffic-dial-default-100-percent, global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region). Weights split traffic inside a group by the [ratio of each endpoint's weight to the total] (global-accelerator-weights-proportion-within-endpoint-group).

**New connections only.** After a dial change, [the updated setting applies to only new connections] (global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only). Do not state a dial range: no fact gives 0 to 100.
plan.table: Truth table, columns Change | Acts on | Open connections: traffic dial | one endpoint group, one Region | stay ([the updated setting applies to only new connections]); weight | one endpoint in a group ([to set values for individual endpoints within], global-accelerator-dials-for-groups-weights-for-endpoints) | stay; weight 0 | that endpoint gets no traffic ([stop sending traffic to an endpoint], global-accelerator-weight-zero-stops-traffic) | stay; endpoint becomes unhealthy | new connections move | stay until the idle timeout ([continues to direct traffic for established connections], global-accelerator-established-connections-until-idle-timeout).
plan.why: Why not just DNS? Resolvers cache a record [according to their time to live (TTL)], outside your control (route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control); with fixed anycast addresses nothing on the client has to change.
plan.exam_signal: 'fail over between Regions within seconds, even though clients cache DNS' points to Global Accelerator, which does not depend on [the IP address caching settings of client devices] (global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: when no endpoint is healthy, and sticky users. At most 75 words. If no healthy endpoint is found [after trying the three closest endpoint groups], [it routes traffic to a random endpoint] (global-accelerator-fails-open-after-three-closest-groups). Idle connections close after [340 seconds] for TCP and [30 seconds] for UDP (global-accelerator-idle-timeout-tcp-340-seconds, global-accelerator-idle-timeout-udp-30-seconds). For stateful applications, client affinity Source IP can [route the user to the same endpoint whenever] the user connects (global-accelerator-client-affinity-source-ip-uses-2-tuple). Keep the 'not guaranteed' scope of that fact.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: health checks move new connections to a healthy Region within seconds. The thing to watch is that open connections stay where they are.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team sets the weight of every endpoint in its standby Region to 0, to keep the standby idle. The primary Region fails. Do new connections go to the standby?' Answer: 'No. Failover looks for a healthy endpoint with a weight above zero ([tries to fail over to a healthy endpoint], global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial). Keep the standby idle with a traffic dial of 0 instead, because for failover [Global Accelerator ignores the traffic dial setting].'

sections.heading: CloudFront bills data sent to viewers and Global Accelerator adds an hourly fee

plan.problem: Moving delivery to the edge changes which network path you pay for. Teams often fear that a CDN adds a second transfer bill.
trace: **Origin to edge.** Transfer from AWS origins such as S3 or a load balancer to CloudFront is [always free when using AWS origins] (cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).
**Edge to viewer.** You pay for [data transfers out from its edge locations] and for [HTTP or HTTPS requests] (cloudfront-price-dimensions-transfer-out-and-requests).

**Trim the edge locations.** A price class lowers prices by [excluding Amazon CloudFront’s more expensive edge locations] (cloudfront-faq-price-classes-exclude-expensive-locations); viewers elsewhere [may experience higher latency] (cloudfront-faq-price-classes-higher-latency-and-billing).

**Accelerator.** Global Accelerator charges [a fixed hourly fee] and a [Data Transfer-Premium fee (DT-Premium)] on top of standard data transfer (global-accelerator-price-fixed-hourly-fee-plus-dt-premium), whether the accelerator is [enabled or disabled] (global-accelerator-price-fixed-fee-enabled-or-disabled).
plan.table: Truth table, columns Item | Charged: S3 or load balancer origin to CloudFront | no ([always free when using AWS origins]); CloudFront to viewers | yes, data out and requests; Origin Shield | extra ([You incur additional charges for using Origin Shield], cloudfront-origin-shield-extra-charges); an HTTP request redirected to HTTPS | both requests ([CloudFront charges for both requests], cloudfront-https-redirect-charges-both-requests); a disabled accelerator | the hourly fee ([enabled or disabled]). No prices or rates in the prose: price facts are volatile.
plan.why: Why can the edge cost less? Each hit is a request that the origin never serves, and CloudFront collapses simultaneous misses into [a single request to your origin server] (cloudfront-faq-cost-collapse-requests).
plan.exam_signal: 'users are only in North America and Europe; reduce delivery cost' points to a price class that leaves out the more expensive locations ([excluding Amazon CloudFront’s more expensive edge locations], cloudfront-faq-price-classes-exclude-expensive-locations).
plan.optional_sentence: If words allow, one sentence after the trace: besides pay-as-you-go, flat-rate plans give one monthly price with [no overage charges] (cloudfront-faq-flat-rate-no-overage-charges). Volatile; never let it decide an answer.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: you pay for data out to viewers, not for fetches from AWS origins. The thing to watch is Origin Shield's extra charge.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A distribution uses a price class that leaves out South America. CloudFront sometimes serves a viewer in South America from a nearby edge location outside the class. Which rate is charged?' Answer: 'The rate of [the least expensive location in your price class] (cloudfront-faq-price-classes-higher-latency-and-billing).'

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten FAQ items from faq below (D12): a can-or-cannot question, a one-clause answer with its fact link, then an AWS quote block of whole sentences from the evidence quote of the same fact, with the FAQ URL. At most 450 words.

traps.belief: CloudFront can serve files from an S3 bucket only if the bucket is public.
traps.truth: With origin access control the bucket stays private: its bucket policy allows the CloudFront service principal only for requests on behalf of your distribution, and viewers cannot use S3 URLs directly.

traps.belief: An origin access identity (OAI) is the recommended way to keep an S3 origin private behind CloudFront.
traps.truth: AWS recommends origin access control (OAC). OAI does not work for all scenarios, for example dynamic requests (PUT, POST or DELETE) to Amazon S3, and an SSE-KMS website bucket needs OAC.

traps.belief: Global Accelerator speeds up a website by caching its images and videos at edge locations.
traps.truth: Global Accelerator proxies TCP and UDP packets at the edge to endpoints that run in AWS Regions; CloudFront is the service that returns cached copies from edge locations.

traps.belief: A Route 53 failover record moves every user to the second Region as fast as Global Accelerator does.
traps.truth: Resolvers and client devices cache DNS answers for their TTL, outside your control. Global Accelerator keeps the same static addresses, does not rely on client caches, and change propagation takes a matter of seconds.

traps.belief: Putting CloudFront in front of S3 adds a second transfer charge, because you pay for S3 to CloudFront and again for CloudFront to the viewer.
traps.truth: Data transfer from AWS origins such as Amazon S3, Elastic Load Balancing or API Gateway to CloudFront is free; you pay CloudFront's data transfer out to viewers.

traps.belief: Putting all headers, cookies and query strings in the cache key helps CloudFront answer more requests from its cache.
traps.truth: To raise the cache hit ratio, AWS says to forward only the query string parameters and cookies that change the response; an origin request policy sends other values to the origin without adding them to the cache key.

traps.belief: Invalidating the changed paths after each release is the recommended way to update files that CloudFront caches.
traps.truth: For frequent updates AWS recommends versioned file names: they also control copies in browsers and proxies and cost less; use invalidation for unexpected cases, and only the first 1,000 paths each month are free.

traps.belief: An Application Load Balancer behind CloudFront must be internet-facing in a public subnet, so that CloudFront can reach it.
traps.truth: With VPC origins, CloudFront delivers content from Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers and EC2 instances in private subnets, and becomes the single point of entry.

traps.belief: When the viewer protocol policy requires HTTPS, the request stays encrypted from CloudFront to the origin as well.
traps.truth: The viewer protocol and the origin protocol are separate settings. To encrypt the origin leg of a custom origin, set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only; CloudFront cannot use HTTPS to an S3 website endpoint.

traps.belief: To protect all the segment files of a video, you must create a signed URL for each file.
traps.truth: Signed cookies give access to multiple restricted files, such as all the files of an HLS video, and the current URLs do not change.

traps.belief: CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge can do the same work; only the price differs.
traps.truth: CloudFront Functions have no network access, no file system access and no access to the request body, and they run in submillisecond time; Lambda@Edge can make network calls and run up to 30 seconds.

traps.belief: When the primary origin fails, an origin group sends every later request, uploads included, to the secondary origin.
traps.truth: CloudFront fails over only when the viewer request method is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, and it tries the primary origin first for every request.

traps.belief: Setting a Region's traffic dial to 0 moves all of its open connections to other Regions at once.
traps.truth: A traffic dial change applies only to new connections; existing connections are not terminated, and established connections keep going to their endpoint until the idle timeout.

Q205 needs a trap id on at least half of the wrong options of the chapter; reuse is allowed. Candidates that fit stems of this chapter:

compare_tables.title: CloudFront or Global Accelerator
compare_tables.rows: Columns: Question | CloudFront | Global Accelerator (3 columns). What it carries: [content that can be sent using the HTTP] or WebSocket protocols (cloudfront-faq-content-types-http-websocket) | [both TCP and UDP protocols] (global-accelerator-faq-protocols-tcp-and-udp). Answers from a cache: yes, [served directly from the CloudFront cache] (cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-definition) | no, it works by [proxying packets at the edge] (global-accelerator-faq-vs-cloudfront-content-types). Addresses that users reach: edge addresses that [vary based on your end user’s location] (route53-faq-cloudfront-ip-addresses-vary-by-location) | [two IPv4 static IP addresses] (global-accelerator-faq-two-static-ipv4-independent-network-zones). Failover between Regions: an origin group, for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS ([only when the HTTP method of the viewer], cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options) | health checks, a failed endpoint out in [less than one minute] (global-accelerator-faq-failover-detect-under-one-minute). Pick it for: [any publicly accessible web application] (cloudfront-dec-consider-for-any-public-web-application) | [gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP] (global-accelerator-faq-good-fit-non-http-static-ip-fast-failover). CloudFront Anycast static IP lists exist since 2024 (Changed recently); do not add them to this table: their facts are frequently changing.
compare_tables.deciding_question: Does the traffic need HTTP caching at the edge, or fixed addresses for TCP or UDP with fast failover between Regions?

compare_tables.title: Origin access control, signed URLs or signed cookies

decision_record.requirement: **Requirement.** Callvale must reduce instance load and latency without making the bucket public, with the LOWEST latency for users around the world. (Last requirement of the Problem plus the qualifier 'lowest latency' of the JSON, in capitals.)
options: a larger web tier and presigned URLs from the Region
CloudFront in front of everything, with private S3 origins and signed URLs (chosen)
decision_record.decision: **Decision.** CloudFront in front of the web application, the static files and the recordings.
reasons_with_facts: Option 1: every request still crosses the internet to one Region, and a presigned URL sends the user straight to S3 with the credentials of the [principal who generated the URL] (s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials), so recordings never come from an edge location.

Option 2: static files leave the instances, but dynamic pages and API calls still make the full trip; CloudFront also speeds up [dynamic, uncacheable workloads like APIs] (cloudfront-dec-dynamic-uncacheable-still-faster).

Option 3: each request goes to the [edge location that provides the lowest latency] (cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge); the buckets stay private, because the bucket policy allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)] for this distribution (cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal); a recording link has [An ending date and time] (cloudfront-dec-signed-url-expiry-restrictions), five minutes in Callvale's case (presigned_playback_minutes, story value).
decision_record.also_added: One sentence after the Decision: three cache behaviors, each with [you specify the one origin] (cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each): static files from callvale-web, recordings from callvale-audio with a trusted key group, everything else to the load balancer with CachingDisabled ([This policy disables caching], cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled); the load balancer's security group allows the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront] (elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg). Their reasons live in How it works.
decision_record.tradeoff: **Trade-off.** Cached files can be old after a release, because CloudFront keeps showing cached content [until the files expire] (cloudfront-removed-origin-file-stays-until-expiry), so each release uses versioned file names: [we recommend that you use a version identifier] (cloudfront-versioned-file-names-recommended). Callvale accepts that.
decision_record.later: One sentence at most: chapter 13 next points callvale.example and app.callvale.example to the distribution with Route 53 alias records; at stage 3 AWS WAF joins the distribution (chapter 08); at stage 4 AWS Global Accelerator gives live.callvale.example fixed addresses in front of the live-audio Network Load Balancers in both Regions, because the bank's firewall team allows fixed addresses only. No new option in the record.

speak.persona: a game studio founder in office hours
speak.prompt: CloudFront or Global Accelerator: which one makes our game faster for players around the world?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both' (J3). Short answer: both bring players onto the AWS network near them; CloudFront caches HTTP content such as patches and web pages, Global Accelerator carries the game's TCP or UDP traffic to your servers through two fixed addresses. How it works: CloudFront answers repeated downloads from the edge; Global Accelerator does not cache, it proxies packets to the nearest healthy Region (say 'proxies', no absolute word). Watch: many games use both: CloudFront for downloads, Global Accelerator for live play. In your case: 'Does your live game traffic use UDP, and how big are your patch files?' Must not say: 'Global Accelerator caches your files'; 'CloudFront carries UDP game traffic'; 'Global Accelerator replaces your load balancers'.

speak.prompt: Every release changes our JavaScript files. Do we invalidate the whole cache each time, or is there a better way?
speak.note: Short answer: put a version in the file names; invalidation is for surprises. How it works: a new name is a new object for CloudFront, browsers and proxies at once; the old copies stay unused; give versioned files a long expiry and the HTML page a short one. Watch: a wildcard invalidation counts as one path, so cost is not the main reason; control of browser and proxy copies is. In your case: 'Does your build tool already add a hash to file names?' Must not say: 'invalidation is free'; 'turn on S3 Versioning'; 'set every TTL to zero'.

speak.prompt: CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge: where should our token check run?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: if the token can be checked with a key that the function holds, CloudFront Functions; if the check must call your user service, Lambda@Edge. How it works: CloudFront Functions run in under a millisecond on the viewer events and cannot call the network; Lambda@Edge can call other services and runs longer, at a higher price. Watch: keep keys in CloudFront KeyValueStore so that you can update them without new code. In your case: 'Is your token a signed JSON web token, or does it need a database lookup?' Must not say: 'CloudFront Functions can call your API'; 'Lambda@Edge is always faster'; 'CloudFront Functions replace Lambda@Edge'.

diagrams.title: A request through CloudFront
diagrams.claim: A request goes to the nearest edge location, and a cache miss travels on through the regional edge cache to the origin.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with four participants: a viewer, an edge location, a regional edge cache and the origin. The viewer's request reaches the edge location, which has no copy. The edge location asks the regional edge cache, which also has no copy, and that cache asks the origin. The object travels back through both caches to the viewer, and both caches keep a copy.
say: DNS routes the request to the edge location that can best serve it, typically the nearest one.
The edge location checks its cache and returns the object when it has a copy.
On a miss, the request goes to the regional edge cache, which has a larger cache.
On a second miss, CloudFront forwards the request to the origin.
As soon as the first byte arrives, CloudFront forwards it to the viewer and adds the object to the cache.
diagrams.note: Size s, four participants (viewer, edge location, regional edge cache, origin), 5 messages plus the returns. In the Markdown steps link step 1 to cloudfront-dns-routes-to-pop ([DNS routes the request to the CloudFront POP] or [nearest CloudFront POP in terms of latency]), step 2 to cloudfront-cache-hit-returns-from-edge, step 3 to cloudfront-rec-larger-cache-than-pop, step 4 to cloudfront-cache-miss-forwards-to-origin, step 5 to cloudfront-first-byte-forwarded-and-cached; the spec say lines equal the Markdown steps without links (L702, L703). No AWS number in labels or steps. The claim has no absolute word, so the caption needs no link (L705).

diagrams.title: CloudFront and Global Accelerator side by side
diagrams.claim: CloudFront answers HTTP requests from edge caches, and Global Accelerator carries TCP and UDP from two static addresses to endpoints in Regions.
diagrams.alt: Two panels. Left, CloudFront: users connect to an edge location that holds cached copies; a miss goes to the origin in one Region. Right, Global Accelerator: users connect to two static anycast addresses at an edge location; traffic crosses the AWS global network to endpoint groups in two Regions, each with a load balancer.
panels: CloudFront: users -> edge location (cache, cloudfront icon) -> origin in a Region (bucket or load balancer)
Global Accelerator: users -> two static addresses at the edge (global-accelerator icon) -> endpoint group in Region 1 and endpoint group in Region 2 (nlb icons)
diagrams.note: Size m, two panels of at most 4 nodes each. Labels a few words, no numbers with units ('two static addresses' is a word count below twelve, allowed). The caption equals the claim; link 'two static addresses' through [two IPv4 static IP addresses] or rephrase so that no hard fact needs a link.

diagrams.title: How does the origin accept only CloudFront?
diagrams.claim: The kind of origin decides how you keep viewers from going around CloudFront.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with three questions. An S3 bucket used through its REST endpoint leads to origin access control. A load balancer or instance that can sit in a private subnet leads to a VPC origin. A load balancer that must stay internet-facing leads to a prefix list and a custom header. Anything else leads to custom headers or origin mutual TLS.
rungs: Is the origin an S3 bucket (not a website endpoint)? -> Origin access control (icon cloudfront or bucket)
Can the ALB, NLB or instance be private? -> VPC origin (icon alb)
Must the load balancer stay internet-facing? -> Prefix list and header (icon alb)
diagrams.note: Ladder: questions at most 9 words, outcomes at most 4 words; no number with a unit in labels. The website-endpoint case leads to the else branch (OAC cannot be used: cloudfront-oac-s3-website-endpoint-not-supported). The claim avoids 'only', so the caption needs no link.

diagrams.title: Callvale before: every request goes to one Region
diagrams.claim: Every request, for a page, a static file or a recording, travels from the user to the load balancer or the bucket in one Region.
diagrams.alt: Before: users on the left, some far from the United States, send every request across the internet to an Application Load Balancer and web instances in US East (N. Virginia). Static files come from the web instances. Recordings come from the private bucket callvale-audio through presigned URLs.
say: Users in the United States and abroad send every request to the one Region.
The web instances serve the pages and the static files.
A recording plays through a presigned URL straight from the bucket.
diagrams.note: Story picture. Steps are story, not AWS rules: no fact link, no number (the 70% and 20% stay in the Context text). Keep the cells of route53-before/after for shared components: users A1, CloudFront B3 (empty here), Application Load Balancer B4; web instances B5; the bucket callvale-audio on the left below the users. Same cells in cloudfront-after (STARTUP A7 rule 13).

diagrams.title: Callvale after: CloudFront in front of everything
diagrams.claim: Users reach the nearest edge location, static files come from its cache, recordings need a signed URL, and dynamic requests go on to the load balancer.
diagrams.alt: After: users on the left connect to CloudFront. Static files come from the edge cache or, on a miss, from the private bucket callvale-web through origin access control. Recordings come from the private bucket callvale-audio, also through origin access control, and need a signed URL. Dynamic requests go on to the Application Load Balancer and the web instances.
say: Users connect to the edge location that gives them the lowest latency.
Static files come from the cache; on a miss CloudFront reads the bucket through origin access control.
A recording needs a signed URL with an ending time.
Dynamic requests go to the load balancer, whose security group allows the CloudFront prefix list.
diagrams.note: At most 8 nodes: users (A1), CloudFront (B3, as in route53-before and route53-after), callvale-web and callvale-audio buckets (left column), Application Load Balancer (B4), web instances (B5). No Route 53 (chapter 13 comes next), no WAF (stage 3), no Global Accelerator (stage 4).
